meta.description: Fields built up from the lake bed and held by stakes and willows, never afloat. One drawn to scale beside a person, with what is known and what is guessed.
meta.og_image_alt: The question over the drawing made for this page: one chinampa and its canal cut across, to one scale for width and height, with its layers, its edge stakes and stones and its willows.

answer: Chinampas are fields built up by hand from the bed of shallow lakes in central Mexico: mud and water plants heaped between canals, held by stakes, stones and willows.

slot.what: One chinampa and its canal cut across, to scale, beside a person 1.7 metres tall. At one dig in Mexico City the buried fields were found up to 0.7 metres high.
slot.alt: A cross-section drawn to scale. A chinampa 4 metres wide rises about half a metre above the water of a canal 2 metres wide, whose floor lies at most 1 metre below the field's edge. The field is built in layers on the lake bed: a base of peat from the lake bottom, then mats of water plants and mud, with canal mud on top. Stones and wooden stakes hold its edges, and willow trees grow along them. A person 1.7 metres tall stands on the field. A small plan shows the whole plot from above, 30 metres long and 4 metres wide.

paras: A chinampa is built up from the bottom of a shallow lake and farmed on its wet, rich soil. In the method recorded from the 16th century on, farmers cut thick mats of water plants in the marsh, towed them to the plot with a wooden hook and heaped them up with earth and mud, then planted living stakes of ahuejote, a willow, along the edges,

found a similar build in about thirty chinampas three metres below today's ground in central Mexico City, at a place once called Ateponazco: peat from the lake bottom as the base, plant waste above it, stones and willow stakes along the sides. The name comes from the Nahuatl chinampan, "on the fence of canes or sticks",
explains.

The water does much of the work. The soil stays moist, canal water is at hand when it dries, and the water softens the night frosts, Virginia Popper writes. Seedlings grow in seedbeds before they are planted out, and in the past mud dredged from the canals kept the soil rich. In the most intensive form, crops grow all year round.
No. Each field was built up from the lake bed and held by stakes, stones and trees, as the
shows. Only the building material floated: thick mats of water plants. In one method that
describes, strips of such a mat were laid where the field was to go and heaped with earth and mud until the heap stood about 2 metres high.

The idea is old. In 1590 the Jesuit José de Acosta described fields in the lake as "fundadas sobre la propia agua", founded on the water itself, and told of a movable planted plot, earth spread on sedge and cattails, sown and carried from place to place (

paras.text: his book, in an edition of 1792

blocks.nav: How much food did chinampas grow for Tenochtitlan?
blocks.h: How much food did chinampas grow for Tenochtitlan?
paras: Nobody knows. One estimate puts it at half to two thirds of the city's food, and a UNAM page says the fields alone could not feed the growing city. The Mexica, often called the Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan on islands in Lake Texcoco in 1325, and the city grew on chinampas,
. Most chinampas lay in the southern lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco, whose water came from springs and was fresh.

By Pedro Armillas's reconstruction of 1981, about 9,000 hectares of fields were made there between about 1300 and 1500, and William Sanders reckoned in 1976 that they could feed 117,000 to 200,000 people, both as reported by
. The half to two thirds is Jeffrey Parsons's estimate, as Popper cites him.
holds that the fields were not large enough to feed the growing city on their own, so some food had to be brought in, through trade and as tribute.

blocks.nav: Where are chinampas still farmed today?
blocks.h: Where are chinampas still farmed today?
paras: In the south of Mexico City: at Xochimilco, San Gregorio Atlapulco, San Luis Tlaxialtemalco, San Pedro Tláhuac and San Andrés Mixquic,

, in the old towns it calls the original peoples (pueblos originarios). Chinamperos and chinamperas farm them with methods handed down by word of mouth, and maize, beans, squash and amaranth still grow there,
The conquest of 1521 was a break, not the end. In the city itself the fields went out of use within fifty years at most,
, while the lake towns kept theirs: the way of building recorded in the 16th century was still in use in the 19th,
A report of

from 2021 counts 18,524 chinampas, 2,824 of them in use. More than a third of those hold greenhouses, pasture, party grounds or football pitches. About half are farmed as chinampas, only 14.4 percent the fully traditional way. Some owners use heavy doses of pesticides and fertilisers, and the growing city presses in, the borough writes. In 2017 the FAO named the chinampa farming of Mexico City a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System,

. In four phases of the borough's project with UNAM's ecological restoration lab and the chinamperos, more than 3,000 metres of canals were cleaned and 20,000 ahuejotes planted, with 30 refuges for the axolotl.
From digs in the old lake beds, from wills and accounts, and from the chinamperos who still build and farm chinampas.
At Ateponazco in 2015, INAH's team under Raúl Barrera Rodríguez mapped plots, canals and furrows. At Xaltocan, in the northern lakes,
mapped buried chinampas from satellite pictures, air photos and digs.
The oldest chinampas known, at Xaltocan, Acatla and Ayotzingo, date from AD 900 to 1200, before Tenochtitlan existed,
and his colleagues write. Their great spread coincides with the rise of the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan.
Nahuatl wills from Culhuacan, most written in 1580 and 1581, leave chinampas to heirs, as

paras: They were built up from the lake bed and held by stakes, stones and trees.
The boats that carry visitors along the canals are trajineras. Chinampas are the fields beside them.
The oldest known fields are older than Tenochtitlan. In the time of the Mexica and their allies they spread over most of the lakes.
Estimates run up to two thirds of its food, and trade and tribute brought food as well.
